lessons.title: Spelling: long and short vowels
lessons.summary: Spell long and short vowels correctly and apply the doubling, single-vowel and f/v, s/z rules that every plural and verb form depends on.

blocks.text: Dutch spelling looks strange at first, but it follows a small set of rules very consistently. The key is the difference between **short** and **long** vowels, and between **closed** and **open** syllables. You will use these rules all the time: every plural (*bomen*, *bussen*) and every verb form (*maken* – *ik maak*) depends on them.
Short and long vowels

The vowels *a, e, o* and *u* each have a short and a long sound. A **short** vowel is always written with **one letter**. A **long** vowel is written with **two letters** (*aa, ee, oo, uu*) – but only in a closed syllable. In an open syllable, one letter is enough.

blocks.caption: The letter i is always short (de vis, fish). Its long partner is always written ie: het dier – de dieren (animal – animals).

blocks.text: Open and closed syllables

A syllable is **closed** when it ends in a consonant (*man, maan, boom*) and **open** when it ends in a vowel (*ma-nen, bo-men*). When you split a word into syllables, a single consonant between two vowels always goes to the next syllable: *ma-nen, bo-men, u-ren*.

**Long vowel:** two letters in a closed syllable (*maan, boom*), one letter in an open syllable (*ma-nen, bo-men*). **Short vowel:** always one letter, and always closed by a consonant in the same syllable – so when an ending is added, that consonant is **doubled** (*bus – bus-sen*).
Adding an ending

items: **Long vowel → write one letter.** The syllable becomes open: *de maan – de manen*, *de boom – de bomen*, *het uur – de uren*, *ik maak – wij maken*.
**Short vowel → double the consonant.** It has to close the first syllable: *de bal – de ballen*, *de bus – de bussen*, *de pen – de pennen*, *ik zit – wij zitten*.
**Two consonants already?** Nothing changes: *de kast – de kasten*, *ik werk – wij werken*.
**Going the other way** (for example from the infinitive to the *ik*-form), do the opposite: *maken* → *ik maak*, *zitten* → *ik zit*.

items.nl: Ik **maak** een taart. Wij **maken** een taart.
items.en: I'm making a cake. We're making a cake.
items.note: maak – ma-ken: open syllable, one a

items.nl: Ik **zit** in de trein. Wij **zitten** in de trein.
items.en: I'm sitting on the train. We're sitting on the train.

items.nl: In onze tuin staat één **boom**, bij de buren staan drie **bomen**.
items.en: There's one tree in our garden; the neighbours have three.

items.nl: De **bus** is vol, maar de andere **bussen** zijn leeg.
items.en: The bus is full, but the other buses are empty.

blocks.text: Say the word slowly in syllables: *bo-men*, *bus-sen*, *le-zen*. If the first syllable ends in a vowel you hear as long, write one letter. If you hear a short vowel, a consonant must close the syllable – so write it twice.
Vowels that never change

Vowels written with two **different** letters – **ie, oe, eu, ui, ij, ei, ou, au** – always stay the same and never cause doubling: *het boek – de boeken*, *de deur – de deuren*, *de tuin – de tuinen*, *de trein – de treinen*. Doubling also never happens after the weak, unstressed *e* (the vowel in English *the*): *ik wandel – wij wandelen*, *ik open – wij openen*.
At the very end of a word, long *a, o* and *u* are written with one letter: *ik ga, zo, nu*. Long *e* keeps two letters: *de zee, twee, mee*.
f/v and s/z

A Dutch word never ends in **v** or **z**. When you hear *v* or *z* before an ending, the short form ends in **f** or **s**: *de brief – de brieven*, *het huis – de huizen*, *ik leef – wij leven*, *ik lees – wij lezen*.

blocks.caption: Not every f or s changes – the spelling follows the pronunciation: de fotograaf – de fotografen, de kous – de kousen.

blocks.text: A few common words switch from a short vowel to a long one in the plural: *de dag – de dagen*, *de weg – de wegen*, *het glas – de glazen*. You will find more of these in *Plural nouns*.

blocks.why: In *ma-ken* the first syllable is open, so the long a needs only one letter. You write *aa* only in a closed syllable: *ik maak*.
*Bus* has a short u. With one s, *bu-sen* would be read with a long u, like *u-ren*.
A Dutch word never ends in v: the stem of *leven* is *leef*.

lessons.title: Subject pronouns
lessons.summary: Choose the right subject pronoun for people and things, including stressed and unstressed forms and informal je versus formal u.

blocks.text: Subject pronouns are the words for *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*. In Dutch the pronoun decides the ending of the verb, so you need to know them well. Several pronouns have two forms: a **stressed** (full) form and an **unstressed** (short) form.

blocks.caption: In speech you will also hear 'k for ik, 't for het, and ie for hij after the verb (Komt ie ook?). Don't use these in formal writing.

blocks.text: The unstressed forms **je, ze, we** are the normal choice in speech and in most writing. Use the stressed forms **jij, zij, wij** when you emphasise or contrast the person.

items.en: What's your name?
We're going to Ghent tomorrow.
You're cooking tonight – I don't have time.

items.nl: **Wij** wonen in Delft, maar **zij** wonen in Breda.
items.en: We live in Delft, but they live in Breda.

blocks.text: The pronoun decides the verb form

blocks.caption: More in Present tense: regular verbs and Zijn, hebben and other irregular verbs.

blocks.text: **Zij/ze** can mean *she* or *they*. The verb shows which one is meant: *zij werkt* (she works), *zij werken* (they work). **Jullie** is the informal plural *you* and always takes the plural verb: *jullie wonen*.
jij/je or u?

Use **jij/je** with friends, family, children, colleagues and people your own age. Use **u** with strangers, older people, customers and in official situations. **u** is used for one person and for several.

**u** takes the verb form with **-t** (*u werkt, u woont, u bent*), and it keeps that -t when it comes after the verb: *Werkt u hier?* Many people in the Netherlands switch to *je* quickly, but if you are not sure, start with *u*. In Belgium *u* is used more widely, and in everyday Flemish speech you will also hear **ge/gij** for 'you'.

items.en: Are you from Amsterdam, sir?
Could you help me, madam?
Are you hungry, guys?

blocks.text: Pronouns for things
For things, use **hij** for a de-word, **het** for a het-word, and **ze** for anything in the plural.

items.nl: Waar is mijn telefoon? – **Hij** ligt op de tafel.
items.en: Where's my phone? – It's on the table.

items.nl: Het boek is spannend. **Het** gaat over Amsterdam.
items.en: The book is exciting. It's about Amsterdam.

items.nl: Ik koop deze schoenen. **Ze** zijn mooi.
items.en: I'm buying these shoes. They're nice.
It's raining and it's cold.

blocks.text: In formal writing, some de-words – especially abstract ones ending in *-heid*, *-ing* or *-tie* – are referred to with **zij**: *de regering ... zij*. In everyday Dutch in the Netherlands, **hij** is normal for de-words.

To introduce or identify someone, use **het** or **dat** + *zijn*, even for people and plurals: *Wie is dat? – Het is mijn broer.* *Dat zijn mijn ouders.* When you go on to say something about the person, switch to *hij* or *zij*: *Hij heet Tom.*
**je** and **ze** can also mean people in general: *In Nederland fiets je overal* (In the Netherlands you cycle everywhere). *Ze zeggen dat het morgen regent* (They say it will rain tomorrow).

blocks.why: *Haar* means *her* (object or possessive). As the subject, use *zij* or *ze*.
In a contrast the pronoun is stressed, so you need the full form *jij*. *Je* is always unstressed.

blocks.wrong: Mijn fiets is kapot. **Het** is oud.
blocks.right: Mijn fiets is kapot. **Hij** is oud.
blocks.why: *Fiets* is a de-word (*de fiets*), so you refer back to it with *hij*.
Only *jij/je* makes the verb drop its -t. With *u*, the -t stays.

lessons.title: Present tense: regular verbs
lessons.summary: Form the present tense of any regular verb, including stems with spelling changes, the dropped -t after jij and stems ending in -t or -d.

blocks.text: Most Dutch verbs are regular in the present tense. Once you can find the **stem** of a verb, you only need three endings: nothing, **-t** or **-en**. The Dutch present covers English *I work*, *I am working* and *do you work?* – there is no extra 'do' or '-ing'. It is also used for the future when a time word makes that clear: *Morgen werk ik thuis* (I'm working from home tomorrow).
Step 1: find the stem

Take the infinitive (the dictionary form, ending in -en) and remove **-en**. Then apply the rules from *Spelling: long and short vowels*, so that the stem keeps the vowel sound of the infinitive. The stem is also the *ik*-form.

rows: long a in a closed syllable → aa
long o in a closed syllable → oo
no double consonant at the end
v at the end → f; long e → ee
z at the end → s; long e → ee

blocks.text: Step 2: add the ending
**ik** + stem. **jij, u, hij, zij, het** + stem + **-t**. **wij, jullie, zij** (plural) + stem + **-en**, which is the same as the infinitive.

blocks.caption: In the plural, the spelling of the infinitive comes back: won-en, zit-ten, le-zen.

items.en: I work in a hospital.
My girlfriend lives in Rotterdam.
He reads the paper every morning.
We're learning Dutch.

blocks.text: jij after the verb: no -t

When **jij** or **je** comes **after** the verb – in questions and after inversion – the verb loses its **-t**: *jij werkt*, but *Werk jij?* This happens only with jij/je. With **u, hij, zij** and **het** the -t stays: *Werkt u?*, *Werkt hij?*

items.en: Are you working tomorrow?
Where do you live?
Tomorrow you're cycling to school.
Do you live in Brussels?

blocks.text: Stems ending in -t or -d

If the stem already ends in **-t**, you never add a second t: *ik zit, jij zit, hij zit* (also *eten – hij eet*, *praten – hij praat*). If the stem ends in **-d**, you still add -t in writing, although you hear no difference: *ik word, jij wordt, hij wordt*. The d belongs to the stem, the t is the ending.

blocks.caption: Other verbs like worden and vinden: rijden (hij rijdt), antwoorden (hij antwoordt), houden (hij houdt).

blocks.text: Want to stress that something is happening right now? Use **aan het** + infinitive: *Ik ben aan het koken* (I'm busy cooking). In most situations the simple present is enough: *Ik kook.*

blocks.why: When *jij/je* follows the verb, the -t disappears.
The stem *zit* already ends in -t. You never add a second t, and a stem never ends in a double consonant.
The stem *word* ends in -d. For *jij, u, hij, zij* and *het* you still add -t: *wordt*.
Dutch has no helper verb like English 'do' in questions. Simply put the main verb first.

lessons.title: Zijn, hebben and other irregular verbs
lessons.summary: Use the present tense of zijn, hebben, the short verbs gaan, staan, slaan, doen and zien, komen, and kunnen, willen, mogen and zullen.

blocks.text: A few very common verbs don't follow the regular pattern exactly. The good news: their plural is always the infinitive (*wij zijn, jullie hebben, zij gaan*), so you only need to learn the singular forms.
zijn and hebben

blocks.caption: As with regular verbs, the -t disappears when jij/je follows the verb: Ben je moe? Heb je tijd?

blocks.text: **zijn:** ik ben, jij bent, hij is. **hebben:** ik heb, jij hebt, hij heeft. With **u** you can say *u hebt* or *u heeft*; for *zijn* use *u bent*.

items.nl: Ik **ben** dertig en ik **heb** twee kinderen.
items.en: I'm thirty and I have two children.
Are you tired?
My mother is a teacher.
Do you have a moment?

items.nl: Wij **hebben** een hond en twee katten.
items.en: We have a dog and two cats.

blocks.text: hebben where English uses 'be'

items: Ik **heb** honger. – I'm hungry.
Ik **heb** dorst. – I'm thirsty.
Ik **heb** het koud / warm. – I'm cold / hot.
Je **hebt** gelijk. – You're right.
We **hebben** haast. – We're in a hurry.
Age uses *zijn*, as in English: Ik **ben** 25 (jaar). – I'm 25.

blocks.text: Short verbs: gaan, staan, slaan, doen, zien

These verbs have a one-syllable infinitive. The stem is the infinitive minus **-n**: *gaa(n) → ga*, *doe(n) → doe*, *zie(n) → zie*. A long a at the end of a word is written with one letter (*ga, sta, sla*). After that, the normal endings follow.

blocks.caption: slaan (to hit) goes like gaan: ik sla, hij slaat, wij slaan.

blocks.text: **komen** (to come) is irregular in another way: its stem has a **short** o. So it is *ik kom, jij komt, hij komt* – not *koom*. The plural is regular: *wij komen*.

items.en: We're going to the cinema tonight.
What do you do at the weekend?
Can you see that tower over there?
Are you from Belgium too?

blocks.text: kunnen, willen, mogen, zullen

**kunnen, willen, mogen** and **zullen** never take -t with hij, zij or het: *hij kan, zij wil, het mag, hij zal*. With jij and u both forms are correct: *jij kunt* or *jij kan*, *jij wilt* or *jij wil*; the form with -t is a bit more formal.

items.en: Can you help me for a moment?
He wants a new phone.
Can I park here?
Shall we have a coffee?

blocks.text: How these verbs combine with a second verb at the end (*Ik kan goed zwemmen*) is explained in *Modal verbs: kunnen, willen, moeten, mogen*. *Moeten* (must) is regular: *ik moet, hij moet*.

blocks.why: Dutch uses *hebben* for hunger, thirst, being cold or hot and being right: *honger hebben, dorst hebben, het koud hebben, gelijk hebben*.
*Willen, kunnen, mogen* and *zullen* have no -t with *hij/zij/het*. You will even hear *hij wilt* from native speakers, but it is not standard Dutch.
*Heeft* is for *hij/zij/het* (and *u*). With *jij* the form is *hebt*.
*Komen* has a short o in the stem: *ik kom, hij komt*.

lessons.title: Articles: de, het and een
lessons.summary: Use de, het and een correctly, recognise the main clues for de- and het-words, and leave out the article where Dutch does.

blocks.text: Dutch has two words for *the*: **de** and **het**. Every noun belongs to one of the two groups: *de man, de stad* are de-words, *het huis, het boek* are het-words. There is only one word for *a/an*: **een** (pronounced like the *a* in *about*).

blocks.caption: There is no plural of een: een huis – huizen (houses).

blocks.text: **de** for de-words, **het** for het-words, **een** for both. In the plural, **every** noun takes **de**: *het huis → de huizen*, *het kind → de kinderen*.

items.en: The train to Utrecht is full.

items.nl: **Het** huis van mijn ouders is oud.
items.en: My parents' house is old.
I'm looking for a flat in Leiden.
The children are playing in the park.

blocks.text: Which nouns are de, which are het?
About two out of three nouns are de-words, but no rule covers them all. Some endings and groups are good clues, though.

rows: people with a gender: **de** man, **de** vrouw, **de** leraar (but: **het** kind)
infinitives used as nouns: **het** eten, **het** zwemmen
many words with ge-, be-, ver-, ont- and no other ending: **het** gesprek, **het** verhaal, **het** begin
blocks.caption: These are tendencies, not guarantees. If you have to guess, guess de – you will be right about two times out of three.

blocks.text: Diminutives (nouns ending in **-je**, *-tje*, *-pje*, *-etje*) are **always** het-words – even when they refer to a person: *het meisje* (the girl), *het mannetje* (the little man).
In a compound noun, the **last** part decides the article: *het huis → het ziekenhuis* (hospital), *de deur → de voordeur* (front door), *de kamer → de slaapkamer* (bedroom).

Always learn a noun together with its article: *het huis*, not just *huis*. Common het-words to learn first: *het huis, het kind, het boek, het jaar, het werk, het geld, het water, het brood, het bier, het weer, het land, het station, het restaurant, het raam, het bed, het idee, het probleem, het woord*.

The article affects other words too. Het-words take **dit/dat** instead of *deze/die* (*dit huis*, but *deze auto*; see *This and that: deze, die, dit, dat*), and you refer back to them with **het** instead of *hij* (see *Subject pronouns*).
Where Dutch and English differ

After *zijn* or *worden*, Dutch normally uses **no article** before a profession, nationality or religion: *Ik ben student.* *Hij is Nederlander.* When there is an adjective, *een* comes back: *Hij is **een** goede kok.*

items.nl: Mijn broer is **kok** en mijn zus is **arts**.
items.en: My brother is a cook and my sister is a doctor.
She's Belgian.
I'm going by train.
items.note: also: met de bus, met de fiets

items.nl: Hoe zeg je dat in **het** Nederlands?
items.en: How do you say that in Dutch?
items.note: but without a preposition: Ik spreek Nederlands.

blocks.why: *Meisje* is a diminutive (-je), and all diminutives are het-words – even when they mean a girl.
Plurals always take *de*, even when the singular is a het-word (*het kind*).
When you simply say what someone's job or status is, Dutch leaves out *een* after *zijn*.

blocks.right: Ik ga **met de trein** naar Gent.
blocks.why: Where English says *by train*, Dutch uses the article: *met de trein, met de bus, met de auto*.

lessons.title: Plural nouns
lessons.summary: Form the plural of Dutch nouns with -en, -s, -'s or -ën, including the spelling changes and the most common irregular plurals.

blocks.text: Dutch has two main plural endings: **-en** and **-s**. Which one a noun takes depends mostly on how the word ends and where the stress falls. Every plural takes the article **de**: *het boek – de boeken*.
Plurals with -en
Most nouns – especially nouns of one syllable and nouns stressed on the last syllable – add **-en**. Apply the spelling rules when you add it.

rows: stressed short vowel: double the n
blocks.caption: These are the rules from Spelling: long and short vowels: bo-men, bus-sen, brie-ven, hui-zen.

blocks.text: Plurals with -s and -'s
Add **-s** to nouns ending in an **unstressed -el, -em, -en, -er** or **-je**, and to many loanwords. Add **'s** to nouns ending in **a, i, o, u** or **y**.

rows: de auto, de taxi, de baby
de auto**'s**, de taxi**'s**, de baby**'s**

blocks.text: The apostrophe in *auto's* keeps the vowel long: *autos* would look like *au-tos* with a short o. Nouns ending in an unstressed -e take -s without an apostrophe: *de tante – de tantes*, *de garage – de garages*. Some family words also take -s: *de broer – de broers*, *de oom – de ooms*.
Nouns ending in -ie and -ee

If the last syllable is a **stressed -ie** or **-ee**, add **-ën**. The two dots (the *trema*) show that a new syllable begins: *de knie – de knieën*, *de zee – de zeeën*, *het idee – de ideeën*, *de industrie – de industrieën*. If -ie is not stressed, add -s: *de familie – de families*, *de studie – de studies*.
Irregular plurals

blocks.caption: Here a short vowel becomes long (dag – dagen, not daggen), the vowel changes (stad – steden) or -eren is added (kind – kinderen). Learn these by heart.

blocks.text: After a number, use the plural: *drie boeken, twee dagen, tien minuten*. But many units of measurement stay singular: *vijf jaar, twee uur, drie euro, twee kilo, tien keer*.

items.en: I have two brothers and three sisters.
items.note: de broer – broers, de zus – zussen

items.en: In Amsterdam you see bikes everywhere.

items.nl: Ik heb mooie **foto's** van de **steden** in België.
items.en: I have lovely photos of the cities in Belgium.
The children are having eggs for breakfast.

items.nl: Na het hardlopen doen mijn **knieën** pijn.
items.en: My knees hurt after running.

blocks.why: After a, i, o, u or y, write *'s*. Without the apostrophe the o would look short.

blocks.wrong: Er staan drie **tafelen** in de kamer.
blocks.right: Er staan drie **tafels** in de kamer.
blocks.why: Nouns ending in an unstressed -el take -s.
*Kind* has an irregular plural: *kinderen*.

blocks.wrong: Ik woon al vijf **jaren** in Gent.
blocks.right: Ik woon al vijf **jaar** in Gent.
blocks.why: After a number, *jaar* normally stays singular, just like *uur*, *euro* and *keer*.

lessons.title: Word order: the verb in second place
lessons.summary: Build main clauses with the finite verb in second position, invert subject and verb when something else comes first, and put a second verb at the end.

blocks.text: One rule shapes almost every Dutch sentence: in a main clause, the conjugated verb – *de persoonsvorm*, the finite verb – is always the **second element**. The first element can be the subject, but it can also be a time, a place, an object or another word.

In a main clause the **finite verb is always in position 2**. If something other than the subject comes first, the subject moves to the place **directly after the verb**. This is called *inversie* (inversion).

blocks.caption: Whatever comes first, the finite verb stays in position 2. A second verb (infinitive or participle) goes to the very end.

items.en: I'm going to the market tomorrow.
Tomorrow I'm going to the market.

items.nl: In de zomer **fietsen** we vaak naar het strand.
items.en: In summer we often cycle to the beach.
I think that book is really good.
Maybe Lisa is coming too.

blocks.text: Position 1 is one **element**, not one word: *Morgen*, *Om negen uur*, *In het centrum van Gent* and *Mijn oudere broer* each fill position 1 on their own. Only one element can stand before the verb.

blocks.why: English allows 'Tomorrow I go', but Dutch doesn't: only one element can come before the verb, so the subject moves behind it.

blocks.text: Words that don't count

The linking words **en, maar, of, want** (and, but, or, because) join two main clauses and don't take up a position. Neither do *ja* and *nee* at the start of an answer. After them, the clause starts as usual. See also *Joining main clauses: en, maar, of, want, dus*.

items.nl: Ik blijf thuis, want ik **ben** ziek.
items.en: I'm staying at home because I'm ill.

items.nl: Ik heb honger, maar eerst **ga** ik douchen.
items.en: I'm hungry, but first I'm going to have a shower.
Yes, I'm coming tomorrow.

blocks.text: A second verb goes to the end

If there is a second verb – an **infinitive** or a **past participle** – it goes to the **end** of the clause. The finite verb in position 2 and the verb at the end form a frame around the rest of the sentence.

items.en: I want to buy a new bike.
Tonight we're going to cook together.
I saw a film yesterday.
items.note: gezien is a past participle (perfect tense)

items.en: Can you give me a call tomorrow?

blocks.why: The infinitive goes to the end of the clause, after the object.

blocks.text: The middle: time – manner – place

In the middle of the sentence, the usual order is **time – manner – place**: *Ik ga morgen (time) met de trein (manner) naar Brussel (place).* There is more about this in *Word order in the middle: time, manner, place and niet*.

blocks.wrong: Ik ga **naar Brussel morgen** met de trein.
blocks.right: Ik ga **morgen met de trein naar Brussel**.
blocks.why: Time comes before manner, and manner before place.

blocks.text: Two other patterns you will meet: questions and commands put the verb **first** (*Kom je ook?* – see *Asking questions*), and in subordinate clauses after words like *dat* and *omdat* the verb moves to the **end** (see *Subordinate clauses: verb at the end*).

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.summary: Ask yes/no questions and question-word questions with the right word order, use waar ... vandaan and waar ... naartoe, and answer with ja, nee or jawel.

blocks.text: Dutch has two kinds of questions: **yes/no questions**, which start with the verb, and **question-word questions**, which start with a word like *wie, wat* or *waar*. In both, the subject comes **right after** the verb. Dutch never uses a helper verb like English *do*.
Yes/no questions
Put the **finite verb first**, then the subject: *Je woont hier.* → *Woon je hier?* Remember: before **jij/je** the verb drops its -t; with **u** it keeps it (*Woont u hier?*).

items.en: Do you live in The Hague?
Do you speak English?
Are you free tonight?
Is the shop open tomorrow?

blocks.text: Questions with a question word
Question word **first**, finite verb **second**, then the subject: *Waar **woon** je?* *Wanneer **begint** de film?*

blocks.caption: Hoe heet je? means 'What's your name?' (literally: how are you called?).

blocks.text: Use **welk** with a singular het-word (*welk huis?*) and **welke** with a de-word or any plural (*welke straat?*, *welke huizen?*). When **wie** or **wat** is itself the subject, the verb follows directly and is singular: *Wie **heeft** mijn pen?* *Wat **is** dat?*
Where from? Where to?
'Where from' and 'where to' are split in two: **waar** goes first, **vandaan** or **naartoe** goes to the **end** of the question.

items.nl: **Waar** kom je **vandaan**? – Ik kom uit Marokko.
items.en: Where are you from? – I'm from Morocco.
Where are you going? – To the beach.

blocks.text: Answering: ja, nee and jawel
Answer a normal question with **ja** or **nee**. To say *yes* to a **negative** question – that is, to contradict it – use **jawel**, often together with *wel*.

items.nl: Heb je een auto? – **Ja**, ik heb een auto. / **Nee**, ik heb geen auto.
items.en: Do you have a car? – Yes, I do. / No, I don't.

items.nl: Kom je niet? – **Jawel**, ik kom wel!
items.en: Aren't you coming? – Yes, I am!

items.nl: Ben je niet moe? – **Nee**, ik ben niet moe.
items.en: Aren't you tired? – No, I'm not.

blocks.text: In speech you will sometimes hear statement order with rising intonation, to check something: *Je komt morgen?* (You're coming tomorrow, right?). In writing, use the verb-first order.

blocks.why: After a question word the verb comes next (position 2), then the subject. Before *je* the -t drops.
'Where ... from' is *waar ... vandaan*, with *vandaan* at the end.
*Fiets* is a de-word, so 'which' is *welke*. *Welk* is only for singular het-words.

lessons.title: Negation: niet and geen
lessons.summary: Choose between niet and geen, put niet in the right place, and use nooit, niemand, niets and nergens without double negatives.

blocks.text: English *no* and *not* correspond to three Dutch words: **nee** (the answer *no*), **geen** (*no, not a, not any* before a noun) and **niet** (*not*). Choosing between *geen* and *niet* is easy once you look at the noun.

rows: before a noun that would have *een* or no article

blocks.text: geen
Use **geen** when the noun would have **een** or **no article at all** in the positive sentence. Use **niet** in all other cases.

**geen** is the same for de-words, het-words and plurals. Nouns with *de*, *het*, *mijn*, *dit* or *die*, names and pronouns are negated with **niet**: *Ik zie de bus niet.* *Ik ken Anna niet.* *Ik zie hem niet.*
Where does niet go?

**niet** usually goes at the **end** of the clause – but **before** an adjective, a prepositional phrase, or a verb at the end (infinitive or participle). It never comes between the subject and the finite verb in a main clause.

rows: at the end of the clause
at the end, after a definite object
at the end, after a time word
blocks.caption: More on the position of niet in Word order in the middle: time, manner, place and niet.

items.en: I don't have any brothers or sisters.
We don't have class today.
The soup isn't hot.

items.nl: Ze gaat morgen **niet** naar haar werk.
items.en: She isn't going to work tomorrow.
I don't want to cook tonight.

items.nl: Woon je in Leiden? – **Nee**, ik woon **niet** in Leiden.
items.en: Do you live in Leiden? – No, I don't.

blocks.text: To contrast one thing with another, put **niet** directly before the word you deny: *Ik wil niet de rode jas, maar de blauwe* (I don't want the red coat, but the blue one).
nooit, niemand, niets, nergens

rows: I can't find my keys anywhere.
Ik rook **niet meer**. We hebben **geen** melk **meer**.
I don't smoke any more. We're out of milk.

blocks.text: **nooit, niemand, niets** and **nergens** are already negative. Standard Dutch never adds a second *niet* or *geen*: *Ik zie niemand*, not *Ik zie niet niemand*.

blocks.why: *een* + noun becomes *geen* + noun. (*Niet één* exists only to stress 'not a single one'.)
The finite verb stays in position 2, so *niet* can't come before it. Here *niet* goes at the end.
*niet* comes before a prepositional phrase like *in Gent*.
*nooit* is already negative; a second negative word makes the sentence non-standard.

lessons.title: Possessive pronouns
lessons.summary: Say whose something is with mijn, jouw, uw, zijn, haar, ons/onze, jullie and hun, and with the van-construction (het huis van Piet, die van mij).

blocks.text: A possessive pronoun (*bezittelijk voornaamwoord*) stands before a noun and says who it belongs to: **mijn** fiets (my bike), **haar** moeder (her mother). It replaces the article: you say *mijn huis*, never *het mijn huis*. Almost all possessives keep the same form before de-words, het-words and plurals.

blocks.caption: The possessive pronouns

blocks.text: The possessive goes before the noun and replaces the article. Only *ons* changes: **ons** before a singular het-word, **onze** before a de-word and before every plural.

items.en: This is my brother Daan.
Where is your bike?
Sir, is this your coat?
items.note: uw: to someone you address as u

items.en: Piet calls his mother every Sunday.

items.nl: Anna woont met **haar** vriend in Gent.
items.en: Anna lives with her boyfriend in Ghent.

items.nl: **Ons** huis is klein, maar **onze** tuin is groot.
items.en: Our house is small, but our garden is big.
items.note: het huis → ons; de tuin → onze

items.en: Is this your car?
items.note: said to two or more people

items.en: My neighbours are selling their house.

blocks.text: Stressed and unstressed forms

Several possessives have a short, unstressed form. **Je** is normal in both speech and writing; use **jouw** only when 'your' is stressed, for example in a contrast. **M'n** and **z'n** are common in speech and informal writing such as messages to friends; in formal writing use *mijn* and *zijn*. **D'r** for *haar* belongs to speech.

items.en: What's your sister called?
Is this your bag or my bag?
items.note: contrast, so the full forms are used

items.en: I'm looking for my keys.
He has lost his phone.
Have you got your tickets?
items.note: when jullie is the subject, the possessive is often je

blocks.text: **Jouw** (your) and **jou** (you, as an object) sound exactly the same. Only *jouw*, with a w, goes before a noun: *jouw boek*, but *voor jou*. In the same way, *mijn* (my) goes before a noun and *mij* (me) does not.
Whose is it? The van-construction

Instead of a possessive you can use **van** + the owner, like English 'of': *het huis van Piet* (Piet's house). This works for every owner, including things: *het dak van het huis* (the roof of the house). With names you can also add **-s**, but Dutch normally writes it without an apostrophe. In informal speech you will also hear *Piet z'n huis* and *Anna d'r tas*; avoid these in writing.

rows: apostrophe after a, i, o, u, y: Anna's, Timo's
after an s-sound only an apostrophe

blocks.text: Mine, yours: van mij, die van mij

To say 'mine', 'yours', 'his' and so on, use **van** + an object pronoun: Die fiets is **van mij** (that bike is mine). To replace a noun that was already mentioned, use **die van** for a de-word or plural and **dat van** for a het-word.

items.nl: Is die tas **van jou**? – Ja, die is **van mij**.
items.en: Is that bag yours? – Yes, it's mine.
These keys are hers.

items.nl: Mijn fiets is oud, maar **die van** Sanne is nieuw.
items.en: My bike is old, but Sanne's is new.

items.nl: Ons huis is klein, maar **dat van** onze buren is groot.
items.en: Our house is small, but our neighbours' is big.

items.nl: Jouw fiets is rood en **de mijne** is blauw.
items.en: Your bike is red and mine is blue.
items.note: de mijne / het mijne: more formal, mainly written

blocks.why: Fiets is a de-word (de fiets), so 'our' is onze. Ons is only used before a singular het-word, as in ons huis.
Jou is an object pronoun (you). Before a noun you need the possessive jouw (or the unstressed je).
Dutch attaches the -s straight to a name, without an apostrophe. Only names ending in a, i, o, u or y take one: Anna's fiets.

lessons.title: Object pronouns
lessons.summary: Use the object pronouns (mij/me, jou/je, u, hem, haar, het, ons, jullie, hen/hun/ze) after verbs and prepositions, and choose hem, het or ze for things.

blocks.text: When a pronoun is the object of a verb (the person or thing the action is done to) or comes after a preposition, Dutch uses a separate object form: *ik* becomes **mij** or **me**, *hij* becomes **hem**. English does the same with I → me and he → him, but Dutch has a stressed and an unstressed form for several persons.

blocks.caption: Subject and object pronouns

blocks.text: Use the object form for the object of a verb and after every preposition. The unstressed forms (**me**, **je**, **ze**) are the normal choice in everyday Dutch; use the stressed forms (**mij**, **jou**, **hen**) for emphasis or contrast.

items.en: Do you remember me?
I'll call you tomorrow.
Can I help you, madam?

items.nl: Waar is Mark? Ik zie **hem** niet.
items.en: Where's Mark? I can't see him.

items.nl: Sanne is jarig. We bezoeken **haar** vanavond.
items.en: It's Sanne's birthday. We're visiting her tonight.
Pieter is helping us with the move.

items.nl: Mijn ouders wonen in Leiden. Ik zie **ze** elk weekend.
items.en: My parents live in Leiden. I see them every weekend.
He means me, not you!

blocks.text: After prepositions

After a preposition such as *met*, *voor*, *bij*, *van*, *naast* or *zonder*, a pronoun is always in the object form. Use the full form when the pronoun is stressed: *Ga je met mij of met hem?* In relaxed speech the short form is also fine: *Ik heb iets voor je.*

items.nl: Wil je met **mij** naar de film?
items.en: Do you want to go to the cinema with me?
This present is for you.
Are you coming to eat at our place on Saturday?
My sister lives next door to him.
I'm going to Rotterdam with them.
items.note: in everyday speech often: met ze

blocks.text: After a preposition, *hem*, *het* and *ze* normally refer to people. For things, Dutch uses a combination with **er** instead: not *met het* but **ermee** (with it). You will learn this in *Erop, daarmee, waarmee: pronominal adverbs*.
Things: hem, het or ze?

For things, the pronoun follows the noun's gender: a de-word becomes **hem** (as a subject: *hij*), a het-word becomes **het**, and every plural becomes **ze**. So English 'it' is often **hem** in Dutch.

items.nl: Waar is mijn telefoon? Ik zie **hem** nergens.
items.en: Where's my phone? I can't see it anywhere.

items.nl: Ik heb een nieuwe fiets. Ik vind **hem** heel mooi.
items.en: I've got a new bike. I think it's really nice.

items.nl: Het boek is goed. Ik lees **het** voor de tweede keer.
items.en: The book is good. I'm reading it for the second time.

items.nl: Ik koop deze schoenen. Ik vind **ze** mooi.
items.en: I'm buying these shoes. I like them.

blocks.text: Them: hen, hun or ze?

For people in the plural, everyday Dutch mostly uses **ze**. Careful written Dutch distinguishes **hen** (direct object, and after a preposition) from **hun** (indirect object, 'to them', without a preposition). For things, use only **ze**.
Where the pronoun goes
An unstressed object pronoun comes straight after the finite verb, or straight after the subject when the subject follows the verb. It comes before time words and before *niet*.

items.en: I'll call you tonight.
I'll call you tonight.
items.note: inversion: the pronoun follows the subject

items.en: I don't know her.

blocks.why: Hij is a subject form. As the object of zien you need the object form hem.
Hun is never a subject in standard Dutch, although you will hear it in casual speech. The subject 'they' is zij or ze.

blocks.wrong: Waar zijn mijn sleutels? Ik zie hen niet.
blocks.right: Waar zijn mijn sleutels? Ik zie ze niet.
blocks.why: Hen and hun are only used for people. Plural things are always ze.

lessons.title: This and that: deze, die, dit, dat
lessons.summary: Point to people and things with deze, die, dit and dat, introduce them with dit is / dit zijn, and use the demonstratives on their own as pronouns.

blocks.text: Demonstratives (*aanwijzende voornaamwoorden*) point at something: 'this', 'that', 'these', 'those'. Dutch has four of them: **deze**, **die**, **dit** and **dat**. Which one you need depends on two questions: is it near or far, and is the noun a de-word or a het-word?

blocks.caption: Demonstratives before a noun

blocks.text: Before a de-word and before any plural: **deze** (near) and **die** (far). Before a singular het-word: **dit** (near) and **dat** (far).

items.en: This coffee is delicious.
This house is too expensive.
Who is that woman?
That restaurant is very good.
These shoes are new.
Do you know those children?
items.note: het kind, but the plural de kinderen → die

blocks.text: *Het*, *dit* and *dat* all end in -t: the t-words go with het-words. And because every plural is a de-word, a plural noun never has *dit* or *dat* directly in front of it.
You also need these words in time expressions: **deze** week, **deze** maand, **deze** zomer, but **dit** weekend and **dit** jaar, because *weekend* and *jaar* are het-words.
Dit is, dat zijn: pointing and introducing

To introduce someone or point something out ('this is …', 'those are …'), use **dit** or **dat** on its own, whatever the noun: de-word, het-word or plural. The verb agrees with the noun that follows: **dit is** + singular, **dit zijn** + plural.

items.en: This is my mother.
That's the train to Utrecht.

items.nl: **Dit zijn** mijn kinderen, Bram en Fleur.
items.en: These are my children, Bram and Fleur.
Those are our new neighbours.
What's that? – It's a stroopwafel.

blocks.why: To introduce someone ('this is …'), use dit or dat, even with a de-word like broer.
After dit or dat, the verb agrees with the noun that follows. Ouders is plural, so: dit zijn.

blocks.text: Deze, die, dit and dat without a noun

A demonstrative can also stand on its own, replacing a noun that is already clear: 'this one', 'that one'. Choose the form the noun would need: **deze/die** for a de-word or plural, **dit/dat** for a het-word. In speech, **die** is also very often used instead of *hij* or *zij* for a person or thing just mentioned.

items.nl: Welke trui vind je mooi? – **Deze** of **die**?
items.en: Which jumper do you like? – This one or that one?

items.nl: Welk brood wil je? – **Dat** daar, graag.
items.en: Which bread would you like? – That one there, please.

items.nl: Ken je Mark? – Ja, **die** woont naast mij.
items.en: Do you know Mark? – Yes, he lives next door to me.

items.nl: Mooie schoenen! – Dank je, **die** zijn nieuw.
items.en: Nice shoes! – Thanks, they're new.

blocks.text: To refer to a whole statement, idea or situation, always use **dat** (or *dit*), never *die*: **Dat** is waar. **Dat** weet ik niet.

items.nl: Ik ga morgen naar Parijs. – O, **dat** is leuk!
items.en: I'm going to Paris tomorrow. – Oh, that's nice!
items.note: dat refers to the whole plan

items.en: I don't know.

blocks.why: Directly before a plural noun you need deze or die, because plurals are de-words. Only in 'dit zijn …' does dit go with a plural.
When you refer to a whole statement, use dat.

lessons.title: Numbers, time and dates
lessons.summary: Count and write numbers, use ordinals, tell the time the Dutch way (half drie = 2:30) and give days, dates and years.

blocks.text: Numbers 1–20

Watch the spelling of **dertien** (13, not *drietien*), **veertien** (14, not *viertien*) and **achttien** (18, with tt). Zero is **nul**. Write **één** with accents only when it could be confused with the article *een*: Ik heb **één** broer (one brother, not two).
Tens, hundreds and thousands

From 21 to 99 the units come first, joined to the tens with **en**: 21 = **eenentwintig** ('one-and-twenty'). The whole number is one word. When *en* follows an e, it gets a diaeresis: **tweeëntwintig**, **drieëntwintig**.

items: 21 **eenentwintig**, 22 **tweeëntwintig**, 23 **drieëntwintig**
35 **vijfendertig**, 48 **achtenveertig**, 99 **negenennegentig**
125 **honderdvijfentwintig**, 250 **tweehonderdvijftig**
1.500 **vijftienhonderd** or **duizend vijfhonderd**
2026 **tweeduizend zesentwintig**

blocks.text: **Honderd** and **duizend** need no *een* in front: 100 = *honderd*, 1.000 = *duizend* (but 1.000.000 = *een miljoen*). Numbers are written as one word up to *duizend*; after *duizend* comes a space: *tweeduizend zesentwintig*. Dutch uses a full stop for thousands and a comma for decimals: 1.500 and €2,50 (*twee euro vijftig*).

After a number, **euro**, **uur**, **jaar**, **kilo** and **keer** stay singular: *drie euro*, *twintig jaar*, *twee keer*. Nouns like *dag*, *week* and *maand* do take the plural: *drie dagen*, *twee weken*.
Ordinal numbers: first, second, third
Ordinals add **-de** up to 19 and **-ste** from 20 upwards. Learn three exceptions by heart: **eerste** (1st), **derde** (3rd) and **achtste** (8th).

blocks.caption: Abbreviate with -e (1e, 2e, 3e) or with the ending (1ste, 2de, 3de, 8ste).

items.en: This is my first Dutch lesson.
We live on the third floor.
items.note: the ground floor is de begane grond

items.nl: Mijn kantoor is op de **achtste** verdieping.
items.en: My office is on the eighth floor.

blocks.text: Telling the time

Ask *Hoe laat is het?* (What time is it?) and answer *Het is … uur*. For full hours use **uur**, which never takes a plural: *Het is drie uur*. Between the hours, Dutch counts from the full hour and also from the half hour – and the half hour belongs to the coming hour.
**Half drie** means 2:30, not 3:30. *Half* always looks ahead to the next hour: it is halfway to three.

blocks.caption: From 3:00 to 4:00

items.nl: Hoe laat is het? – Het is **half acht**.
items.en: What time is it? – It's half past seven.

items.nl: De trein vertrekt om **kwart over negen**.
items.en: The train leaves at quarter past nine.

items.nl: Mijn les begint om **vijf voor half negen**.
items.en: My lesson starts at twenty-five past eight.

items.nl: De film begint om **tien over half tien**.
items.en: The film starts at twenty to ten.
We eat at six o'clock.

blocks.text: For :20 and :40 you will also hear **twintig over drie** (3:20) and **twintig voor vier** (3:40), especially in Belgium. Timetables use the 24-hour clock: 14.30 uur (*veertien uur dertig*). To make the part of the day clear, add **'s ochtends**, **'s middags**, **'s avonds** or **'s nachts**: om acht uur 's avonds (8 p.m.).

blocks.wrong: Het is 3.30 uur, dus het is half drie.
blocks.right: Het is 3.30 uur, dus het is half vier.
blocks.why: Half points forward to the next hour: 3:30 is half vier. Half drie is 2:30.
In clock times, uur never takes the plural.

blocks.text: Days, months and dates

items: Days: **maandag** (Monday), **dinsdag** (Tuesday), **woensdag** (Wednesday), **donderdag** (Thursday), **vrijdag** (Friday), **zaterdag** (Saturday), **zondag** (Sunday)
Months: **januari**, **februari**, **maart**, **april**, **mei**, **juni**, **juli**, **augustus**, **september**, **oktober**, **november**, **december**
Seasons: **de lente** (spring, also *het voorjaar*), **de zomer**, **de herfst** (autumn, also *het najaar*), **de winter**

blocks.text: Days and months are written with a small letter. In a date the day comes before the month: *op 3 mei* (said: *op drie mei*). Use **op** with days and dates, **in** with months, years and seasons, and **om** with clock times.

items.en: My birthday is on 12 April.
The shop is closed on Sundays.
We're going to Spain in August.
My father was born in 1965.

items.nl: De hoeveelste is het vandaag? – De **vierde**.
items.en: What's the date today? – The fourth.

blocks.text: Write dates as *3 mei 2026* or *3-5-2026* (day, month, year). Years before 2000 are said in hundreds: 1965 = *negentienhonderdvijfenzestig*. From 2000 on, say *tweeduizend*: 2026 = *tweeduizend zesentwintig*. With the month, use the plain number (*op drie mei*); without it, use the ordinal (*op de derde*).

blocks.wrong: Ik ben op Maandag 3 Mei jarig.
blocks.right: Ik ben op maandag 3 mei jarig.
blocks.why: Days and months are not capitalised in Dutch.
Units come before tens, joined with en and written as one word: vier-en-twintig.

lessons.title: Modal verbs: kunnen, willen, moeten, mogen
lessons.summary: Say what you can, want, have to and are allowed to do with kunnen, willen, moeten and mogen, with the modal in second place and the infinitive at the end.

blocks.text: Modal verbs (*modale werkwoorden*) add a meaning such as ability, wish, obligation or permission to another verb: Ik **kan** zwemmen (I can swim). The four basic ones are **kunnen**, **willen**, **moeten** and **mogen**. Their present tense is irregular, so learn the forms by heart.

blocks.caption: Present tense of the four modal verbs

blocks.text: There is never a -t after *hij*, *zij* or *het*: **hij kan**, **hij wil**, **zij mag**. With *jij* and *u*, both *kunt/kan* and *wilt/wil* are correct; *kunt* and *wilt* sound a little more careful. When *jij/je* comes after the verb, the -t disappears: **Kun** je …? **Wil** je …?
The modal verb is the finite verb, so it stands in **second place**. The other verb goes to the **end** of the clause as a bare infinitive, without *te*.

items.en: I can cook well.
He wants to live in Utrecht.
We have to get up early tomorrow.
May I open the window?
Tomorrow I have to work.
items.note: inversion: the modal stays in second place

items.en: I can't come tomorrow.

blocks.text: What each verb means

rows: can, be able to; be possible
Ik **kan** goed zwemmen. Je **kunt** ook met de bus gaan.

blocks.text: Make a request polite with **graag**, or turn it into a question with **mag** or **kun**: Ik wil **graag** een koffie. **Mag** ik de rekening? **Kun** je me helpen? A plain *Ik wil …* can sound rather blunt.
Must not and don't have to

English 'must not' (it is forbidden) is **niet mogen**: Je mag hier niet roken. English 'don't have to' is **niet hoeven te**: Je hoeft niet te betalen. *Niet moeten* is not a ban but advice: 'you shouldn't'.

items.en: You mustn't cycle here.
You don't have to come.
You shouldn't work so hard.

blocks.text: Modal verbs without a second verb

When the meaning is obvious, Dutch often leaves out the infinitive – usually *gaan*, *doen* or *hebben*. This is especially common with a direction: *Ik moet naar huis* means *Ik moet naar huis gaan*.

items.en: I have to go to the doctor.
Would you like a cup of tea?
Could I have a glass of water?
That's not possible.
That's not allowed.
Do you speak French?

blocks.why: The infinitive goes to the very end of the clause, after everything else.
After kunnen, willen, moeten and mogen the infinitive has no te.

blocks.wrong: Hij wilt een nieuwe auto kopen.
blocks.right: Hij wil een nieuwe auto kopen.
blocks.why: With hij, zij and het there is never a -t: hij wil, hij kan, hij mag. Only jij and u can take wilt and kunt.

lessons.title: Basic prepositions of place and time
lessons.summary: Say where something is, where you are going and when something happens with the most common prepositions, including naar versus bij and om, op and in for time.

blocks.text: Prepositions (*voorzetsels*) are short words like *in*, *op* and *naar* that link a noun to the rest of the sentence. They rarely translate one-to-one: English 'at' can be *op*, *bij*, *aan* or *om*. Learn them in fixed combinations rather than word by word.
Where is it? Place

rows: Het station ligt **tussen** de kerk en het park.
Ik woon **bij** het station. Ik ben **bij** mijn oma.

blocks.text: **op** = on top of a surface. **aan** = attached to or hanging on something, such as a wall or the ceiling. **bij** = at or near a place, or at someone's home or business.
Fixed combinations

items: **op** school, **op** het werk, **op** kantoor, **op** het station, **op** straat, **op** de markt
**in** de stad, **in** het park, **in** de winkel, **in** Nederland, **in** Antwerpen
streets and canals: Ik woon **in** de Kerkstraat. Ze wonen **aan** de Prinsengracht.
islands: **op** Texel, **op** Curaçao
**aan** tafel (at the table), **aan** zee (at the seaside)
**bij** de bakker, **bij** de dokter; Ik werk **bij** een bank (I work at a bank).
**thuis** (at home) – no preposition!

blocks.text: Where to and where from? Direction
**naar** = movement towards a place or person (to). **bij** = being at a place or person (at). **uit** = from (origin) or out of. **van … naar** = from … to (a route).

items.en: I'm going to the doctor.
I'm at the doctor's.
We're going to my grandmother's on Sunday.
I'm going home. I'm at home.
He's from Morocco.

items.nl: Ze haalt de melk **uit** de koelkast.
items.en: She takes the milk out of the fridge.

items.nl: De trein **van** Utrecht **naar** Den Haag is vol.
items.en: The train from Utrecht to The Hague is full.

blocks.text: With, for, of: met, voor, van

items.en: I'm going by train.
items.note: transport: met de trein, met de bus, met de auto; also op de fiets

items.en: I live with my girlfriend.
This present is for you.

items.nl: Dit is een foto **van** mijn familie.
items.en: This is a photo of my family.

items.nl: Ik heb een brief **van** de gemeente.
items.en: I've got a letter from the council.

blocks.text: When? Time
Clock time → **om**. Day or date → **op**. Month, year or season → **in**.

items.nl: De winkel gaat **om** negen uur open.
items.en: The shop opens at nine o'clock.
I don't work on Saturdays.

items.nl: **In** de winter is het vroeg donker.
items.en: In winter it gets dark early.
I work from Monday to Friday.
After the lesson we have coffee.
The train leaves in ten minutes.

blocks.text: No preposition is needed with *vandaag*, *morgen*, *vanavond*, *volgende week* or with **'s ochtends**, **'s middags**, **'s avonds** and **'s nachts**: Ik werk 's avonds (I work in the evenings).

blocks.wrong: Ik ga morgen bij mijn oma.
blocks.right: Ik ga morgen naar mijn oma.
blocks.why: Going to someone is naar. Bij is for being at their place: Ik ben bij mijn oma.

blocks.wrong: De les begint op negen uur.
blocks.right: De les begint om negen uur.
blocks.why: Clock times always take om.
Thuis means 'at home' and is used without a preposition. 'Going home' is naar huis.
The country or city you come from takes uit.

lessons.title: There is / there are: er is and er zijn
lessons.summary: Say that something exists or can be found somewhere with er is, er zijn and er ligt/staat/hangt/zit, in statements, questions and negatives.

blocks.text: To say that something exists or can be found somewhere, Dutch uses **er** + a form of **zijn**: *er is* (there is) and *er zijn* (there are). The little word *er* has no meaning of its own here; it just fills the first place. The real subject comes after the verb, so the verb agrees with that noun.
**Er is** + a singular or uncountable noun. **Er zijn** + a plural noun.

rows: Er **is** een supermarkt in de straat.
Er **zijn** drie supermarkten in de stad.

items.nl: Er **is** een bakker om de hoek.
items.en: There's a baker's around the corner.
There are a lot of bikes in Amsterdam.

items.nl: Er **is** een probleem met de trein.
items.en: There's a problem with the train.

items.nl: Er **zijn** twintig studenten in mijn klas.
items.en: There are twenty students in my class.

blocks.text: Use *er is / er zijn* with an indefinite noun: after *een*, *geen*, a number, *veel*, or with no article. For a specific, known thing, start with the noun itself: *De supermarkt is om de hoek* (the supermarket is around the corner).
Questions and inversion

In a yes/no question the verb comes first and *er* follows it: **Is er** …? **Zijn er** …? When a sentence starts with a time word, *er* also moves behind the verb. After a place at the start, *er* is often left out.

items.nl: **Is er** een supermarkt in de buurt?
items.en: Is there a supermarket nearby?
Are there any more questions?

items.nl: Hoeveel kamers **zijn er** in het huis?
items.en: How many rooms are there in the house?

items.nl: Morgen **is er** een feest bij Lotte.
items.en: There's a party at Lotte's tomorrow.
There are lots of students in Utrecht.
items.note: er is optional after a place at the start

items.en: What's the matter?

blocks.text: No, none, nobody: er is geen, er is niemand

To say 'there isn't a …' or 'there aren't any …', use **geen**: Er is geen melk. Er zijn geen kaartjes meer. Also very common: **er is niemand** (there's nobody) and **er is niets** (there's nothing).

items.en: There's no bread left.
There are no tickets left.
There's nobody home.
Isn't there any wifi here?

blocks.text: Er ligt, er staat, er hangt, er zit

Dutch often prefers a verb of position to *zijn*. The choice depends on how the thing is placed, and the verb still agrees with the noun after it: *er ligt* een boek, *er liggen* twee boeken. You will meet these verbs all the time.

rows: things standing upright or on their base: bottles, glasses, furniture, buildings
Er **staat** een fles water op tafel.
things lying flat: books, phones, keys; also towns and cities
Er **liggen** twee boeken op de bank.
Er **hangt** een klok aan de muur.
things inside something: a container, a drink, a bag

blocks.wrong: Er heeft een kat in de tuin.
blocks.right: Er is een kat in de tuin.
blocks.why: 'There is' is always er is or er zijn. Dutch never uses hebben in this construction.

blocks.wrong: Er is veel mensen op het plein.
blocks.right: Er zijn veel mensen op het plein.
blocks.why: The verb agrees with the noun after it. Mensen is plural, so: er zijn.
The finite verb must be in second place. When morgen comes first, is comes before er.

blocks.wrong: Het is een supermarkt om de hoek.
blocks.right: Er is een supermarkt om de hoek.
blocks.why: Het is means 'it is' and identifies something (Het is een supermarkt = It's a supermarket). To say that something exists somewhere, use er is.

lessons.title: The future with gaan
lessons.summary: Talk about plans and the near future with gaan + infinitive, or with the present tense and a time word, using the correct word order.

blocks.text: To talk about the future, Dutch mostly uses two simple patterns: **gaan + infinitive** (like English 'going to') and the plain **present tense** with a time word. A third option, *zullen*, comes in *The future: present tense, gaan and zullen*.
The forms of gaan
**gaan** is the finite verb in **second place**; the main verb goes to the **end** of the clause as an infinitive, without *te*.

items.en: I'm going to cook pasta tonight.
We're getting married in June.
My parents are going to buy a new house.
What are you doing this weekend?
Are you going to study in Leuven next year?

items.nl: Kijk naar de lucht: het **gaat regenen**.
items.en: Look at the sky: it's going to rain.
items.note: a prediction based on what you see now

blocks.text: Use *gaan* + infinitive for plans and intentions, and for things you can already see coming. It often also means 'go and do': *Ik ga even boodschappen doen* (I'm just going to do the shopping).
The present tense for the future
When a time word makes the future clear, Dutch very often uses the plain **present tense**, where English needs 'will' or 'going to'.

items.en: I'll call you tomorrow.
The course starts next week.
My sister is coming later.
We're flying to Lisbon on Saturday.
I'll help you.

blocks.caption: Useful time words for the future

blocks.text: Word order

blocks.caption: gaan in second place, the infinitive at the end

blocks.text: Time comes before place: *Ik ga zaterdag in Utrecht winkelen.* *Niet* comes just before the infinitive: *Ik ga morgen niet werken.* In a yes/no question, *gaan* comes first.
With a direction (*naar* …) you don't need a second verb: *Ik ga morgen naar Utrecht* already means 'I'm going to Utrecht tomorrow'. Don't add another *gaan* at the end.

blocks.why: The infinitive goes to the very end of the clause; the time word comes before it.

blocks.wrong: Morgen ik ga naar de markt.
blocks.right: Morgen ga ik naar de markt.
blocks.why: The finite verb is always in second place. When morgen comes first, the subject moves behind the verb.
Gaan takes a bare infinitive, without te.

blocks.wrong: Ik ga morgen naar Utrecht gaan.
blocks.why: Gaan + naar already expresses the plan and the movement; don't add a second gaan.

exercises.explanation: In ma-nen the first syllable is open, so the long a is written with one letter. 'Mannen' (men) has a short a, and 'maanen' doubles a vowel in an open syllable.

exercises.prompt: In onze straat staan veel ___. (de boom)
exercises.explanation: Boom has a long oo. In the plural bo-men the first syllable is open, so one o is enough. A double m would make the o short.

exercises.prompt: Bij het station staan drie ___. (de bus)
exercises.explanation: Bus has a short u. The s is doubled so that it closes the first syllable: bus-sen. With one s (bu-sen) the u would be read as long.

exercises.prompt: Which verb has a short vowel in its first syllable?
exercises.explanation: The double t in zit-ten closes the first syllable, so the i is short. In ma-ken, lo-pen and wo-nen the syllable ends in a single vowel letter, so the vowel is long.
Remove -en: lev. A Dutch word cannot end in v, so it becomes f, and the long e needs two letters in the closed syllable: ik leef. 'Leeft' is the form for jij and hij.

exercises.prompt: De ___ in deze straat zijn heel oud. (het huis)
exercises.explanation: Between two vowels you hear and write z: het huis – de huizen. 'Ui' is written with two different letters, so the consonant is never doubled.
Lezen minus -en is lez. A word cannot end in z, so it becomes s, and the long e is doubled in the closed syllable: ik lees. 'Les' (lesson) has a short e.
Remove -en: ik wandel. The e in -del is the weak, unstressed e, and a consonant is never doubled after it.
Dag is an exception: its plural has a long a (da-gen), written with one a in the open syllable. The same happens in weg – wegen and glas – glazen.
The form 'ben' only goes with 'ik'. 'Jij' would need 'bent', 'hij' needs 'is' and 'wij' needs 'zijn'.

exercises.prompt: Dat is Anna. ___ is mijn zus.
exercises.explanation: The subject pronoun for a woman is 'ze' (or 'zij'). 'Haar' is the object or possessive form and cannot be the subject.

exercises.prompt: Mijn broer woont in Gent. ___ is student.
exercises.explanation: Mijn broer is a man, so the subject pronoun is hij. 'Hem' is the object form and cannot be the subject.

exercises.prompt: Peter en ik wonen in Utrecht. ___ hebben een kat.
exercises.explanation: Peter and I together are 'we', so the subject is wij (or we). Zij/ze would mean other people.

exercises.prompt: Het huis is groot. ___ heeft vier slaapkamers.
exercises.explanation: Huis is a het-word (het huis), so you refer back to it with het.

exercises.prompt: Waar is de sleutel? – ___ ligt op de tafel.
exercises.explanation: Sleutel is a de-word (de sleutel). A de-word thing is referred to with hij, not het.

exercises.prompt: Ik heb nieuwe schoenen. ___ zijn heel mooi.
exercises.explanation: For things in the plural, use ze: ze zijn heel mooi.

exercises.prompt: You ask an older man you don't know where he lives. Which question is best?
exercises.explanation: Use u with strangers and older people. With u the verb keeps its -t, even after the verb: Waar woont u?
When the pronoun is stressed or contrasted, use the full form jij. 'Je' is always unstressed, 'jou' is the object form and 'jouw' means 'your'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'They work in Den Haag'?
exercises.explanation: Zij can mean 'she' or 'they'; the verb shows which. Zij werken (plural verb) means 'they work', zij werkt means 'she works'.
With ik, use the bare stem: werken minus -en gives werk.
Regular verbs add -t in the third person singular: hij woont. The stem 'woon' is only for 'ik'.
With wij, jullie and zij (plural) the verb is the same as the infinitive: wij spelen.
Zitten has the stem zit. It already ends in -t, so you don't add another one: jij zit, hij zit.
The stem of lezen is lees (z becomes s, long e is doubled). For zij (mijn zus) add -t: leest.
When jij comes after the verb, the -t is dropped: Kook jij vanavond?
The -t only disappears before jij/je. With u it stays: Woont u in Antwerpen?
The stem word ends in -d, but for hij you still add -t: hij wordt. It sounds the same as word, but the spelling is different.

exercises.prompt: Wat ___ jij van mijn nieuwe fiets? (vinden)
exercises.explanation: The stem is vind. Jij comes after the verb here, so there is no -t: Wat vind jij? (But in normal order: jij vindt.)

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'Do you work here?'
exercises.explanation: Dutch does not use 'do' in questions: the main verb goes first. Before je the verb drops its -t: Werk je hier?
The verb 'zijn' with 'ik' is 'ben'. 'Bent' goes with 'jij' and 'is' with 'hij/zij/het'.
With 'jij' the verb 'hebben' takes the form 'hebt'. 'Heb' is for 'ik' and 'heeft' for 'hij/zij/het'.
Anna is a she (zij), and with hij/zij/het hebben becomes heeft.
When the verb comes before 'jij', it loses its -t: 'Ben jij moe?'. This happens whenever jij/je follows the verb, as in questions.
Doen has the stem doe. It is jij doet, but when jij follows the verb the -t drops: Wat doe jij?

exercises.prompt: Ik ___ honger. Zullen we iets eten?
exercises.explanation: Dutch says 'I have hunger': ik heb honger. The same goes for dorst hebben (to be thirsty) and het koud hebben (to be cold).

exercises.prompt: Hoe laat ___ de trein uit Amsterdam? (komen)
exercises.explanation: Komen has a short o in its stem: ik kom, hij komt (not koom). De trein is singular, so: komt.
Kunnen is irregular: ik kan, hij kan, with no -t for hij/zij/het. 'Kunt' is only for jij and u.
Mogen: ik mag, jij mag, hij mag, wij mogen. The singular has a different vowel and never takes -t.
With u the verb keeps its -t, even when it comes first: Hebt u even een momentje? (Heeft u ...? is also correct.) Only jij/je drops the -t.
'Huis' is a het-word: het huis. 'Die' and 'deze' are only used with de-words; het-words take 'dat' and 'dit'.

exercises.prompt: ___ station van Utrecht is heel groot.
exercises.explanation: Station is a het-word: het station. Learn every noun together with its article.
'Boek' is a het-word: het boek. 'De', 'deze' and 'die' are used with de-words.

exercises.prompt: Ik zie ___ kinderen in het park.
exercises.explanation: Plurals always take de, even when the singular is a het-word: het kind – de kinderen. 'Een' has no plural.
All diminutives ending in -je are het-words, so it is 'het meisje'. 'Vrouw' and 'man' are de-words.
Nouns ending in -ing are de-words: de vergadering.

exercises.prompt: Hoe zeg je 'thank you' in ___ Nederlands?
exercises.explanation: Names of languages are het-words: het Nederlands, het Engels.

exercises.prompt: ___ ziekenhuis is aan het eind van de straat. (ziekenhuis = zieken + huis)
exercises.explanation: In a compound, the last part decides the article. It is het huis, so it is het ziekenhuis.
Nouns ending in -ment are usually het-words: het document. Nouns in -teit, -tie and -ing are de-words.

exercises.prompt: Choose the most natural translation: 'My sister is a nurse.'
exercises.explanation: When you state someone's profession after zijn, Dutch normally leaves out the article: Mijn zus is verpleegkundige.
Most Dutch nouns form the plural with -en: boek becomes boeken. A consonant is only doubled after a short vowel written with one letter; 'oe' is written with two letters, so the k stays single.

exercises.prompt: In de keuken staan vier ___. (de stoel)
exercises.explanation: Most nouns take -en: de stoel – de stoelen. After oe the consonant is never doubled.
Nouns ending in a, i, o, u or y take an apostrophe before the plural -s, which keeps the vowel long: auto's. After 'twee' the noun must be plural.

exercises.prompt: Er liggen twee ___ op de tafel. (de sleutel)
exercises.explanation: Nouns ending in an unstressed -el, -em, -en, -er or -je take -s: de sleutel – de sleutels. ('Sleutelen' is a verb: to tinker.)

exercises.prompt: Er zijn drie ___ in de klas.
exercises.explanation: 'Het kind' has an irregular plural: kinderen. 'Kinders' is not standard Dutch.
Between two vowels you hear a v, so the f becomes v: de brief – de brieven.

exercises.prompt: Utrecht en Gent zijn mooie ___. (de stad)
exercises.explanation: Stad has an irregular plural: the vowel changes and becomes long, de steden.

exercises.prompt: Ik heb pijn in mijn ___. (de knie, plural)
exercises.explanation: Nouns ending in a stressed -ie or -ee take -ën. The trema (the two dots) shows that -en starts a new syllable: knie-en.

exercises.prompt: Voor de taart heb ik zes ___ nodig. (het ei)
exercises.explanation: Ei belongs to the small group with -eren, like kind – kinderen: het ei – de eieren.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the most natural?
choices: Ik woon al vijf jaar in Utrecht.
Ik woon al vijf jaren in Utrecht.
Ik woon al vijf jaars in Utrecht.
exercises.explanation: After a number, jaar normally stays singular, like uur, euro, kilo and keer: vijf jaar, twee uur.
The conjugated verb must be in second position. When 'morgen' comes first, the verb follows immediately and the subject moves after it.
After a fronted time word the verb stays in second position, so subject and verb invert: 'Morgen ga ik'.
Dutch main clauses are verb-second. With 'vandaag' in first position, the verb 'eet' must come next, before the subject.

exercises.prompt: In de zomer ___ vaak naar het strand.
exercises.explanation: 'In de zomer' fills position 1, so the verb comes second and the subject (we) follows it: In de zomer gaan we ...
The time phrase fills first position, so the verb comes second and the subject follows: 'Om negen uur begint de les'. 'De les' is singular, so 'begint'.
Even when the object (dat boek) comes first, the verb stays in position 2 and the subject follows: Dat boek vind ik heel goed.
En, maar, of and want don't count as a position. After want the clause starts normally, with the subject first: want ik ben ziek.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I want to read a book tonight.'
choices: Ik wil lezen vanavond een boek.
Ik vanavond wil een boek lezen.
Vanavond ik wil een boek lezen.
Ik wil vanavond een boek lezen.
exercises.explanation: The finite verb (wil) is in position 2 and the infinitive (lezen) goes to the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has the most natural word order?
choices: Ik ga naar Leiden morgen met de bus.
Ik ga morgen met de bus naar Leiden.
Morgen ik ga met de bus naar Leiden.
Ik ga met de bus morgen naar Leiden.
exercises.explanation: In the middle of the sentence Dutch prefers time – manner – place: morgen – met de bus – naar Leiden.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'Yesterday I bought a new coat.'
choices: Gisteren ik heb een nieuwe jas gekocht.
Gisteren heb ik gekocht een nieuwe jas.
Gisteren heb ik een nieuwe jas gekocht.
Gisteren heb gekocht ik een nieuwe jas.
exercises.explanation: Heb is the finite verb, so it comes second, directly followed by the subject. The past participle gekocht goes to the end.
'Waar' asks about a place: Waar woon je? means Where do you live?

exercises.prompt: ___ is die man? – Dat is mijn buurman.
exercises.explanation: Wie asks about a person: Wie is die man? (Who is that man?)
Dutch asks for a name with 'hoe': Hoe heet jij? (also: Hoe heet je?) literally means How are you called?
Yes/no questions start with the verb, and before 'jij' the verb drops its -t: 'Kom jij uit Nederland?'.

exercises.prompt: ___ kinderen heb je? – Twee, een zoon en een dochter.
exercises.explanation: Hoeveel asks about a number or amount: Hoeveel kinderen heb je? (How many children do you have?)

exercises.prompt: ___ begint de les? – Om half negen.
exercises.explanation: Hoe laat asks for a clock time: Hoe laat begint de les? (What time does the class start?)

exercises.prompt: ___ huis is van jullie? – Het grote huis op de hoek.
exercises.explanation: Huis is a singular het-word, so 'which' is welk: Welk huis? With de-words and plurals use welke.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'Why are you tired?'
exercises.explanation: Question word first, then the verb, then the subject. Before je the verb drops its -t: Waarom ben je moe?
'Where ... from' is waar ... vandaan: Waar kom je vandaan? Naartoe and heen mean 'to'.

exercises.prompt: Kom je vanavond niet? – ___, ik kom wel!
exercises.explanation: To contradict a negative question (to say 'yes, I am'), use jawel, often with wel.
'Geen' negates an indefinite noun (een auto becomes geen auto). 'Niet' is used to negate verbs, adjectives and definite nouns.
'Niet' negates the verb here; there is no indefinite noun to negate, so 'geen' is impossible.
'Koffie' is an indefinite mass noun, so it is negated with 'geen': wij drinken geen koffie.
Duur is an adjective, so it is negated with niet, which goes right before it.
In a neutral sentence 'niet' comes after a definite object like 'de man' (it only goes before it in a contrast: niet de man, maar de vrouw). 'Geen' is only used with indefinite nouns.

exercises.prompt: Ik ben ___ student meer; ik werk nu.
exercises.explanation: Student has no article here (ik ben student), so it is negated with geen: ik ben geen student meer.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I don't live in Rotterdam.'
exercises.explanation: Niet goes before a prepositional phrase such as in Rotterdam: Ik woon niet in Rotterdam.

exercises.prompt: Is er iemand thuis? – Nee, er is ___ thuis.
exercises.explanation: Niemand means nobody: er is niemand thuis (nobody is home). Niets is nothing, nergens nowhere, nooit never.
Nergens means nowhere or not anywhere: Ik kan mijn telefoon nergens vinden (I can't find my phone anywhere).

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I can't come tomorrow.'
exercises.explanation: Niet goes before an infinitive at the end of the clause: Ik kan morgen niet komen.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I never eat meat.'
exercises.explanation: Nooit is already negative, so there is no extra geen or niet. The verb stays in position 2: Ik eet nooit vlees.

exercises.prompt: Ik heb een boek. Dit is ___ boek.
exercises.explanation: 'Mijn' is the possessive form (my). 'Mij' is the object pronoun (me) and cannot be used before a noun.

exercises.prompt: Dit is Jan. ___ fiets is rood.
exercises.explanation: 'Zijn' means his and refers back to Jan. 'Haar' means her, and 'hij' and 'hem' are personal pronouns, not possessives.

exercises.prompt: Anna woont in Gent. ___ broer woont in Brussel.
exercises.explanation: Anna is a woman, so 'her' is haar: haar broer. Zijn means his and hun means their.
Meneer (sir) shows you are speaking politely, so you address him with u and the possessive is uw.

exercises.prompt: Tom en Lisa hebben twee kinderen. ___ kinderen zitten op school in Utrecht.
exercises.explanation: Tom and Lisa together are 'they', so 'their' is hun. Hen is an object pronoun (them), never a possessive.

exercises.prompt: Wij hebben een hond. ___ hond heet Max.
exercises.explanation: Before a de-word like 'de hond' the possessive is 'onze'. 'Ons' is only used before het-words.

exercises.prompt: Wij wonen in Leiden. ___ huis staat vlak bij het station.
exercises.explanation: Huis is a singular het-word (het huis), so 'our' is ons. Onze is for de-words and plurals.

exercises.prompt: Is die fiets van jou? – Ja, die is van ___.
exercises.explanation: After a preposition like van you need the object pronoun: van mij (mine). Mijn and m'n only go directly before a noun.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct spelling of 'Peter's bike':
exercises.explanation: Dutch attaches the -s straight to the name without an apostrophe: Peters fiets. An apostrophe is only used after a, i, o, u or y (Anna's fiets) or on its own after an s-sound (Hans' fiets).

exercises.prompt: Mijn huis is klein, maar ___ van mijn broer is groot.
exercises.explanation: Dat van replaces a het-word: dat van mijn broer = het huis van mijn broer. For a de-word or a plural you would say die van.
As the object of the sentence, 'hij' changes to 'hem': ik zie hem (I see him).

exercises.prompt: Mijn zus woont in Amsterdam. Ik bezoek ___ vaak.
exercises.explanation: Mijn zus is the object here, so 'her' is haar. Zij is the subject form.
After a preposition such as bij you need the object form: bij ons. Wij and we are subject forms, and onze is a possessive (our).
After the preposition voor you need the object form jou (or unstressed je). Jouw means 'your' and goes before a noun; jullie is for more than one person.

exercises.prompt: Waar is mijn telefoon? Ik zie ___ nergens.
exercises.explanation: Telefoon is a de-word, so 'it' as an object is hem. Het is only for het-words, and hij is a subject form.

exercises.prompt: Ik heb een nieuw boek. Ik lees ___ vanavond.
exercises.explanation: Boek is a het-word (het boek), so 'it' is het.

exercises.prompt: Waar zijn mijn sleutels? Ik zie ___ niet.
exercises.explanation: Sleutels are plural things, and plural things are always ze. Hen and hun are only used for people.
The subject 'they' is zij or ze. Hun and hen are object forms; 'hun wonen' is heard in casual speech but is not standard Dutch.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has the normal word order?
exercises.explanation: An unstressed object pronoun like je comes right after the finite verb, before time words such as morgen: Ik bel je morgen.

exercises.prompt: Ik geef ___ een cadeau. (them – careful written Dutch)
exercises.explanation: In careful written Dutch the indirect object 'to them' (without a preposition) is hun. Hen is for the direct object and after prepositions; in speech most people simply say ze.
Huis is a het-word and 'this' means near, so you use dit: dit huis.
Man is a de-word and he is over there (far), so you use die: die man.
Appels is plural, and plurals always take deze or die. 'These' (near) is deze.
To introduce someone ('this is …') you use dit on its own, even though zus is a de-word.
With dit or dat + zijn, the verb agrees with the noun after it. Ouders is plural, so: dit zijn.

exercises.prompt: Welke fiets is van jou? – ___ daar, de rode.
exercises.explanation: Fiets is a de-word, so a stand-alone 'that one' is die.

exercises.prompt: Ik ga morgen naar Parijs. – O, ___ is leuk!
exercises.explanation: To refer to a whole statement or plan, Dutch uses dat: dat is leuk.
Meisje is a diminutive and therefore a het-word: dat meisje. In the plural it would be die meisjes or deze meisjes.

exercises.prompt: How do you write 25 in Dutch?
exercises.explanation: The units come first, joined to the tens with en, all in one word: vijfentwintig.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of 22?
exercises.explanation: Twee + en + twintig is one word, with a diaeresis on the e of en to show that a new syllable starts: tweeëntwintig.
Third is derde, one of the irregular ordinals (with eerste and achtste). Dertiende means thirteenth.

exercises.prompt: Mijn kantoor is op de ___ verdieping. (8th)
exercises.explanation: Acht is an exception: it takes -ste, giving achtste. Achttiende means 18th.
Half points forward to the next hour: 2:30 is half drie. Half twee would be 1:30.
6:45 is a quarter before seven: kwart voor zeven. Half zeven would be 6:30.
8:25 is five minutes before half negen (8:30): vijf voor half negen.
4:40 is ten minutes after half vijf (4:30): tien over half vijf. You may also hear twintig voor vijf.
Dates and days take op: op 12 mei, op maandag. In is for months and years, om for clock times.

choices: Op Maandag 3 Mei ben ik jarig.
Op maandag 3 Mei ben ik jarig.
Op Maandag 3 mei ben ik jarig.
Op maandag 3 mei ben ik jarig.
exercises.explanation: Days and months take a small letter in Dutch: maandag, mei. Only the first word of the sentence gets a capital.
With ik the form of kunnen is kan: ik kan goed zwemmen. Kunt goes with jij and u, and kun is only used when jij/je follows the verb (Kun je zwemmen?).

exercises.prompt: Mijn kinderen ___ om acht uur naar bed. (moeten)
exercises.explanation: Mijn kinderen is plural, so the verb takes the plural form, which is the same as the infinitive: moeten. The infinitive gaan can be left out because naar bed shows the direction.
Mogen has the same form for ik, jij, u and hij: mag, without -t. (Moogt is an old or Belgian form that goes with gij.)
After a modal verb like 'willen', the second verb goes to the end of the sentence as an infinitive: lezen.
The modal verb 'mogen' (to be allowed to) with 'ik' is 'mag': Mag ik hier zitten?
When jij/je comes after the verb, the -t is dropped: Kun jij …? (Kan jij …? is also used.)
The modal wil is in second place and the infinitive leren goes to the end, without te.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I have to go home.'
exercises.explanation: 'Have to' is moeten. After a modal, the infinitive gaan can be left out when a direction (naar huis) is given.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'You mustn't park here.' (it is forbidden)
choices: Je hoeft hier niet te parkeren.
exercises.explanation: A ban ('must not') is niet mogen: je mag hier niet parkeren. Je hoeft niet te … means 'you don't have to'.
For living in a city you use 'in': hij woont in Amsterdam. 'Naar' expresses movement, not location.
Movement toward a place uses 'naar': ik ga naar school (I am going to school).
Something inside the fridge is 'in de koelkast'. 'Aan', 'naar' and 'uit' do not fit with 'staat' here.
Clock times take om: om acht uur.
Months, years and seasons take in: in augustus.
Being at school is op school. Naar school is used for going there.
Something hanging on a wall is aan de muur. Op is for things lying or standing on top of a surface.

exercises.prompt: Ik ben vanavond ___ mijn ouders. (at my parents' place)
exercises.explanation: Being at someone's home is bij: bij mijn ouders. Naar is only for going there.

exercises.prompt: Hij komt ___ Turkije, maar hij woont nu in Rotterdam.
exercises.explanation: The country you come from takes uit: hij komt uit Turkije.
Going home is naar huis. Thuis means 'at home' and is used without a preposition: ik ben thuis.
With a singular noun ('een kat') you use 'er is'. 'Er zijn' is for plurals, and 'hebben' is never used in this construction.
'Veel mensen' is plural, so the verb must be plural: er zijn.

exercises.prompt: ___ er een apotheek in de buurt?
exercises.explanation: In a yes/no question the verb comes first. Een apotheek is singular, so: Is er een apotheek in de buurt?
'Melk' is a singular mass noun, so it takes 'er is'. The verb must also stay in second position.

exercises.prompt: Hoeveel studenten ___ er in de klas?
exercises.explanation: Hoeveel studenten is plural, so the verb is zijn: Hoeveel studenten zijn er in de klas?
When vandaag comes first, the verb must still be in second place, so er moves behind it: Vandaag is er geen les. Les is singular, so is.

exercises.prompt: Er ___ een mooie lamp boven de tafel.
exercises.explanation: A lamp above the table is hanging, so the verb is hangen: er hangt een lamp.

exercises.prompt: Er ___ twee boeken op de bank.
exercises.explanation: Books lying on the sofa take liggen, and twee boeken is plural: er liggen.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'There is a bakery around the corner.'
choices: Het is een bakkerij om de hoek.
Er heeft een bakkerij om de hoek.
Er zijn een bakkerij om de hoek.
Er is een bakkerij om de hoek.
exercises.explanation: 'There is' + a singular noun is er is. Het is means 'it is', and hebben is never used for 'there is'.
With ik the form of gaan is ga: ik ga morgen tennissen. Ging is the past tense.
When jij comes after the verb, the -t is dropped: Ga jij …?

exercises.prompt: Kijk naar de lucht! Het ___ regenen.
exercises.explanation: Gaan + infinitive predicts something you can see coming. With het the form is gaat: het gaat regenen.

exercises.prompt: Mijn broer gaat volgend jaar in Leuven ___.
exercises.explanation: After gaan the main verb is a bare infinitive at the end of the clause: studeren, without te.
Ga is in second place, the time word follows, and the infinitive werken goes to the end without te.
When volgende week comes first, ga stays in second place and the subject ik follows it. The infinitive verhuizen goes to the end.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I'll call you tomorrow.'
exercises.explanation: With a time word, Dutch simply uses the present tense: ik bel je morgen. With gaan, the infinitive would have to go to the end (Ik ga je morgen bellen).
Niet comes just before the infinitive at the end: Ik ga morgen niet werken.

exercises.prompt: Ik ga ___ jaar in Gent wonen. (next)
exercises.explanation: Jaar is a het-word, so without an article there is no -e: volgend jaar. Compare volgende week (de week).
